displayQuote: Plans are worthless, but planning is everything

meta.title: Who really said "Plans are worthless, but planning is everything"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Eisenhower really did say it — on 14 Nov 1957, in the Public Papers. But he called it an Army saying he’d heard, and he never claimed to coin it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Plans are worthless, but planning is everything'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified to Eisenhower's 14 Nov 1957 speech in the Public Papers of the Presidents — but he presented the line as old Army lore, not his own.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1890–1969 · 34th U.S. President and General of the Army
answer.sourceLine: Eisenhower spoke these exact words at the National Defense Executive Reserve Conference in Washington, D.C., on 14 November 1957, and the transcript in the Public Papers of the Presidents carries them verbatim. He was quoting, not coining — he introduced the line as “the statement I heard long ago in the Army,” and Quote Investigator ↗ finds he had used an earlier form of it in a 1950 letter, crediting an anonymous soldier.

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: Remarks at the National Defense Executive Reserve Conference
Public Papers of the Presidents of the United States: Dwight D. Eisenhower, 1957, p. 818
Not claimed — Eisenhower called it “the statement I heard long ago in the Army”

source.excerpt:
I tell this story to illustrate the truth of the statement I heard long ago in the Army: Plans are worthless, but planning is everything. There is a very great distinction because when you are planning for an emergency you must start with this one thing: the very definition of “emergency” is that it is unexpected, therefore it is not going to happen the way you are planning.

So, the first thing you do is to take all the plans off the top shelf and throw them out the window and start once more. But if you haven’t been planning you can’t start to work, intelligently at least.
trail: 31 December 1950 — Eisenhower writes to Hamilton Fish Armstrong: “Peace-time plans are of no particular value, but peace-time planning is indispensable,” crediting “a very successful soldier” (Quote Investigator ↗).
14 November 1957 — As President, he uses the compact form in Washington, D.C.: “Plans are worthless, but planning is everything” (full transcript ↗).

1962 — Richard Nixon’s Six Crises prints a variant wording, “In preparing for battle I have always found that plans are useless, but planning is indispensable,” and credits it to Eisenhower as one of his favourites — the earliest documented appearance of that phrasing (Quote Investigator ↗).
Today — Wikiquote lists the sentence in its sourced 1950s section, citing Public Papers of the Presidents… 1957, p. 818 (Wikiquote ↗).

author.name: Dwight D. Eisenhower
author.kicker: The man who said it — and said he didn’t coin it
author.heading: Who was Dwight D. Eisenhower?
author.bio: Born in Denison, Texas in 1890, Dwight David Eisenhower rose to Supreme Commander of the Allied Expeditionary Force, the officer who ran the Normandy invasion, before serving as the 34th President of the United States from 1953 to 1961. His professional life was, more than almost anyone’s, a life of staff planning — which is why a throwaway line about plans became one of the sentences he is most often quoted for in management and military writing. Characteristically, he refused the credit for it: he said he had picked it up in the Army long before.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right; the authorship claim usually is not. Eisenhower spoke the sentence, but he presented it as something he had heard, and the wording widely printed under his name is not the wording the transcript records — it is a variant first documented in Richard Nixon’s 1962 Six Crises.

items.why: In the speech itself he introduces it as “the statement I heard long ago in the Army” (transcript ↗). Quote Investigator concludes he used and popularised the saying but “disclaimed credit by ascribing the words to an anonymous soldier” (QI ↗).

items.who: “In preparing for battle I have always found that plans are useless, but planning is indispensable”
items.why: This widely quoted sentence is first documented in Richard Nixon’s 1962 book Six Crises, where Nixon presents it as one of President Eisenhower’s favourites and credits Eisenhower for it. No earlier source for that wording is known, and it is not the wording the 1957 Eisenhower transcript records (QI ↗).

Having repeated the saying, Nixon started collecting it: Quote Investigator records a 1975 Christian Science Monitor item attributing “plans are useless, but planning is indispensable” to Nixon himself (QI ↗).

“No plan survives first contact with the enemy” is a separate, older adage condensed from Moltke’s 1871 wording; Quote Investigator treats it as a thematic antecedent, not the source of Eisenhower’s sentence (QI on Moltke ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Eisenhower genuinely said these exact words on 14 November 1957 — the transcript ↗ proves it — but he was passing along Army lore, and the earliest evidence Quote Investigator ↗ reports for the proverb is Eisenhower’s own letter of 31 December 1950, where he again credited an unnamed soldier.

context.heading: Why he was saying it
lead: The audience was a Cold War emergency-mobilization conference, and Eisenhower’s point was practical rather than aphoristic. “When you are planning for an emergency you must start with this one thing,” he told them: “the very definition of ‘emergency’ is that it is unexpected, therefore it is not going to happen the way you are planning.”

His conclusion was not that planning is a waste. It was the opposite — you throw the binder away and start again, and you can only do that quickly if you have already done the thinking. “If you haven’t been planning you can’t start to work, intelligently at least.” The line has since been absorbed into management, military and startup folklore, usually shorn of the paragraph that explains it.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator documents an earlier Eisenhower use in a letter to Hamilton Fish Armstrong dated 31 December 1950: “Peace-time plans are of no particular value, but peace-time planning is indispensable.” There too he credited someone else — “a very successful soldier.”
Per Quote Investigator, the 2012 reference work The Dictionary of Modern Proverbs recorded that 1950 letter as the earliest evidence it found for the proverb.
